question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. With its cast trigger on the stack, I copy that trigger with [Lithoform Engine]. Then I untap Lithoform Engine with [Voltaic Key] and use it again to copy [Emrakul, the Promised End] itself as a permanent spell. How many of my opponent's turns do I control, do I get a second Emrakul, and does copying the Emrakul spell give me another control-a-turn trigger?
answer:
You control exactly one of your opponent's turns from all of this, you do get a second Emrakul, the Promised End (as a token), but copying the Emrakul, the Promised End spell itself does NOT generate another "gain control" trigger.

Walking through it: When you cast Emrakul, the Promised End, its triggered ability "When you cast this spell, you gain control of target opponent during that player's next turn. After that turn, that player takes an extra turn" triggers and goes on the stack above the Emrakul, the Promised End spell itself. Using Lithoform Engine's first ability ({2}, {T}: Copy target activated or triggered ability you control) on that trigger puts a copy of that triggered ability on the stack (707.10, 707.10e); you may choose a new target for the copy, but presumably it still targets the same opponent.

When both the copy and the original trigger resolve, each independently tries to (a) apply a "you gain control of target opponent during that player's next turn" effect and (b) create a delayed triggered ability that says "after that turn, that player takes an extra turn" (603.7h). Per Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #14, multiple player-controlling effects that affect the same player overwrite each other -- only the last one created actually governs that turn -- but each resolution still independently creates its own extra-turn delayed trigger, and those are not overwritten; per rule 500.7 extra turns are simply added one at a time. So you end up controlling your opponent's next turn only once (the two 'gain control' effects collapse into one, since both target the same turn), but your opponent will subsequently take two extra turns of their own (one queued up by each resolution), taken one after the other under rule 500.7.

Separately, tapping Voltaic Key to untap Lithoform Engine and then using its third ability ({4}, {T}: Copy target permanent spell you control) on the Emrakul, the Promised End spell while it's still on the stack does give you a second Emrakul, the Promised End: per rule 111.13, a copy of a permanent spell becomes a token with the copied spell's characteristics as it resolves, so you'll end up with two 13/13 Eldrazi named Emrakul, the Promised End on the battlefield (the original plus the token copy).

However, this does NOT grant you a second "gain control" trigger. Emrakul, the Promised End's relevant ability triggers specifically "when you cast this spell," and a copy of a spell is never cast -- rule 707.10 states "a copy of a spell isn't cast," and Lithoform Engine ruling #6 confirms that creating a copy this way won't cause abilities that trigger on casting a spell to trigger. So the copied Emrakul, the Promised End spell resolving into a token generates no additional control-a-turn trigger.

Note: I'm assuming a standard two-player game with a single opponent throughout, since the question refers to "my opponent" in the singular; in a multiplayer game the two copies of the trigger could in principle target different opponents (since you may choose new targets for the Lithoform Engine copy), in which case you would control one turn from each of the two different opponents instead of doubling up on a single opponent's turn.

question: An opponent controls an untapped [Trinisphere], and I have a permanent that makes my green spells cost {1} less. I want to cast [Awaken the Woods] for value. If I cast it with X=0, what does it cost and what do I get, and what X should I actually choose?
answer:
If you cast Awaken the Woods with X=0, the spell's cost starts as {0}{G}{G} (i.e. just {G}{G}). Your green-cost-reduction permanent tries to reduce the generic portion by {1}, but there's no generic mana left to reduce, so it stays at {G}{G} (2 total mana). Since that's less than three mana, Trinisphere's replacement effect kicks in and forces the total cost up to three mana — {G}{G} plus one more mana of any color/colorless, i.e. effectively {1}{G}{G}. You end up paying 3 mana total for X=0, which means you create zero Forest Dryad tokens (Awaken the Woods creates X tokens) — a complete waste of the extra mana Trinisphere forced on you.

The X you should actually choose is X=2. Here's why: the value of X you announce when casting (rule 107.3a) is the same X used both in the mana cost and in the spell's effect text (rule 107.3i), so a higher X both raises the nominal cost and increases the number of tokens you get. With X=2, the mana cost starts at {2}{G}{G}. Your reduction effect knocks {1} off the generic portion, leaving {1}{G}{G} — a mana component of 3. Per Trinisphere's own ruling, its tax only applies 'if the mana component of the spell's cost is less than three mana' (Trinisphere ruling #0); since {1}{G}{G} is already exactly three mana, Trinisphere's effect doesn't trigger at all. So you pay the same {1}{G}{G} (3 total mana) as you would for a wasted X=0 cast, but this time you get 2 Forest Dryad 1/1 land creature tokens instead of 0.

Going further, X=1 also gets bumped by Trinisphere to a final cost of {1}{G}{G} (since {1}{G}{G} reduced by {1} becomes {G}{G}, only 2 mana, still under three, so Trinisphere pads it back to 3), giving you just 1 token for the same 3-mana price — strictly worse than X=2. X=3 would cost {2}{G}{G} (4 mana, no Trinisphere tax since the reduced cost {2}{G}{G} is already ≥3) for 3 tokens, which is more mana for more value but not 'free' the way X=2 is. So X=2 is the sweet spot: it's the largest X where Trinisphere's tax has no additional bite beyond what your own cost reduction already offsets, giving you the most tokens per mana spent given the fixed 3-mana floor Trinisphere imposes.

All of this follows the total-cost calculation order in rule 601.2f (mana cost, then reductions, then Trinisphere's own instruction to apply its tax last per Trinisphere ruling #0), and the mana value of the spell itself is fixed at casting time by rule 202.3e/107.3a regardless of how much you actually pay.

question: [Grist, the Hunger Tide] is in my graveyard. Can I return it with [Animate Dead], and what happens?
answer:
Yes, you can target Grist, the Hunger Tide with Animate Dead, but the end result is that you get it back for only a moment before you're forced to sacrifice it. While Grist is in your graveyard it has the text "As long as Grist isn't on the battlefield, it's a 1/1 Insect creature in addition to its other types," so in the graveyard it is a Legendary Planeswalker Creature — Grist Insect (Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #1), and Animate Dead (which enchants a "creature card in a graveyard") can legally target it and be cast.

When Animate Dead resolves and enters the battlefield attached to Grist's card in the graveyard, its own triggered ability fires: "When this Aura enters, if it's on the battlefield, it loses 'enchant creature card in a graveyard' and gains 'enchant creature put onto the battlefield with this Aura.' Return enchanted creature card to the battlefield under your control and attach this Aura to it." This returns Grist, the Hunger Tide to the battlefield under your control. However, the instant Grist is on the battlefield, its "as long as Grist isn't on the battlefield" clause stops applying, so it is no longer a creature at all — it's just a planeswalker (Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #1). Because Animate Dead's enchant ability now requires it to be attached to a creature, and Grist is not a creature once it's on the battlefield, Animate Dead cannot legally attach to it. This is exactly the situation covered by Animate Dead ruling #4: when the creature "can't legally be enchanted by Animate Dead for another reason, Animate Dead won't be able to attach to it. It will be put into the graveyard as a state-based action, causing its delayed triggered ability to trigger." That delayed trigger is Animate Dead's "When this Aura leaves the battlefield, that creature's controller sacrifices it" clause. Since Grist, the Hunger Tide is still on the battlefield (as a planeswalker) when that trigger resolves, you must sacrifice it.

Net result: casting Animate Dead on Grist, the Hunger Tide does return it to the battlefield momentarily under your control, but Animate Dead immediately falls off (going to your graveyard) because Grist stops being a creature, and you then have to sacrifice Grist, the Hunger Tide via Animate Dead's leaves-the-battlefield trigger. You don't get any lasting use out of Grist's loyalty abilities, though you would get any "enters the battlefield" style triggers, if it had any (it doesn't). This assumes normal timing where Animate Dead resolves fully before any other spells/abilities intervene; if some other effect changed Grist's characteristics (e.g., made it a creature while on the battlefield) before the state-based action check, the outcome could differ, but nothing in the provided card text does that.
